source: Tao Te Ching, tr. James Legge, 1891 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 39). Public domain. Each line was checked character for character against Project Gutenberg eBook #216 and sacred-texts.com; see docs/design/research.md.

lines.text: Let movement go on, and the condition of rest will gradually arise.
Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of movement.
The soft overcomes the hard; and the weak the strong.
The highest excellence is like (that of) water.
The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new.
He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches his legs does not walk (easily).
He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty.
Purity and stillness give the correct law to all under heaven.
the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong.
Who can (make) the muddy water (clear)? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear.
